glosses: …, wasn't it? (digging for a half-remembered fact)
patterns.usage_note: Casual recollection: you are groping for something you once knew, either checking with your listener or muttering to yourself. だっけ is the shape after a noun and after the ta-stems that voice た to だ (飲んだっけ); elsewhere it surfaces as たっけ (控えたっけ, 出したっけ). It also rides on the non-past through ん (明日[あした]は休[やす]みなんだっけ, これ、どうやって開[あ]けるんだっけ), and unlike its sibling たもんだ, which only reminisces, だっけ can either check one half-remembered fact or, with よく and a time frame, drift into the same fond recollection.

examples.ruby: 次[つぎ]の打[う]ち合[あ]わせって、来週[らいしゅう]の水曜[すいよう]だっけ。
examples.english: Our next meeting is Wednesday next week, right?

examples.ruby: あの角[かど]のラーメン屋[や]、名前[なまえ]なんて言[い]ったっけ。
examples.english: That ramen place on the corner — what was it called again?

examples.ruby: 彼[かれ]の連絡先[れんらくさき]、確[たし]かノートに控[ひか]えたっけ。
examples.english: His contact details — did I write them down in my notebook?

glosses: we'd always (do); those were the days when I'd (do)
patterns.usage_note: Looks back fondly on something done again and again over a stretch of past time, so it sits naturally with よく or 毎日; for a one-off past experience 〜たことがある is normally the right choice instead. The realization is だもん／だもの after the ta-stems that voice た to だ (泳いだもんだ) and たもん／たもの elsewhere, with もん the more casual contraction of もの. Do not confuse it with the excuse-making 〜んだもん ('because, you know'), which attaches to plain forms and nouns and is a different construction.

examples.ruby: 子供[こども]の頃[ころ]は、日[ひ]が暮[く]れるまで川[かわ]で泳[およ]いだもんだ。
examples.english: As a kid I'd swim in the river until the sun went down.

examples.ruby: 昔[むかし]の職場[しょくば]では、終電[しゅうでん]まで資料[しりょう]を集[あつ]めたものだ。
examples.english: At my old workplace we'd be digging up material right up to the last train.

examples.ruby: 祖母[そぼ]の家[いえ]までは、よく一人[ひとり]で電車[でんしゃ]に乗[の]って行[い]ったものだ。
examples.english: I used to ride the train out to my grandmother's house all on my own.
